name: Mahé
tagline: Granite-boulder beaches and jungle peaks on the Indian Ocean.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Sep, Oct, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: April-May and October-November bring the calmest seas and clearest skies between the trade winds; expect windier water and swell at the height of each monsoon.

ourTake.lede: Mahé is where you land and where you should linger a day or two, but the Seychelles reveal themselves on Praslin and La Digue, plan the inter-island hops in. On Mahé itself, trade Beau Vallon's crowds for the harder-to-reach south, Anse Intendance and Petite Anse are the beaches you'll remember. Rent a car and do the cross-island mountain road; the Morne Seychellois forest is the island's overlooked half.
ourTake.comeIf: You want granite-boulder beaches and rare seclusion, visa-free, with Mumbai close.
ourTake.skipIf: You want nightlife or sightseeing; the islands reward stillness and swimming.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: North Island, a Luxury Collection Resort
items.area: North Island (private island, ~30 km off Mahé; access by helicopter or boat)
credentials: Marriott's The Luxury Collection, the marque's Seychelles flagship
Named among the world's most beautiful hotels; World Luxury Hotel Awards winner
items.description: The icon of the Seychelles, a barefoot private island of just eleven hand-built villas, where the whole island is yours and the price of entry buys near-total seclusion.

items.name: Six Senses Zil Pasyon
items.area: Félicité (private island, near La Digue; boat or helicopter transfer)
credentials: Condé Nast Traveler, Triple Crown Award; Hot List on opening
Tatler Spa Guide Award
items.description: Thirty pool villas scattered across a granite-boulder island, the most complete expression of Six Senses wellness in the Indian Ocean, with a spa carved into the rocks.

items.name: Fregate Island Private
items.area: Frégate Island (private island, easternmost of the granitic Seychelles; helicopter transfer)
credentials: Oetker Collection, the group's Indian Ocean private island
Anse Victorin named among the world's best beaches (The Times; CNN Travel)
items.description: An Oetker Collection private island of sixteen clifftop villas above Anse Victorin, a beach repeatedly called one of the world's best, run as much as a conservation estate as a resort.

items.name: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles
items.area: Mahé (Petite Anse / Baie Lazare, southwest coast)
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide, Four Star
MICHELIN Guide hotel selection (a hotel listing, not a dining star)
items.description: The benchmark for polished, family-capable luxury on the main island, treehouse-style villas terraced down a jungle hillside to a private horseshoe bay.

items.name: Anantara Maia Seychelles Villas
credentials: Anantara / Minor Hotels flagship, award-winning gardens and spa
Recognised across the luxury travel trade for its all-villa, butler-led model
items.description: Thirty villas on a private peninsula wrapped in thirty acres of jungle, a butler-for-every-villa, all-inclusive sanctuary designed by Bill Bensley.

items.name: Raffles Seychelles
items.area: Praslin (Anse Volbert / Baie Sainte Anne, north coast)
credentials: World Travel Awards, Indian Ocean's Leading Luxury Resort and Leading Honeymoon Resort (multiple years)
Forbes Travel Guide-recognised; Condé Nast Traveller Hot List (opening)
items.description: Praslin's grande dame, 86 hillside pool villas above the beach, with the storied Raffles service and easy reach of the Vallée de Mai and La Digue.

items.name: Constance Ephélia
items.area: Mahé (Port Launay, northwest coast, on the Port Launay Marine Park)
credentials: Constance Hotels flagship, Condé Nast Traveler Readers' Choice Awards nominee
Award-winning Spa de Constance (one of the region's largest)
items.description: A sprawling estate across two beaches and 120 hectares, home to one of the largest spas in the Indian Ocean, the most versatile big resort on Mahé.

items.name: Mango House Seychelles, LXR Hotels & Resorts
items.area: Mahé (Anse aux Poules Bleues, Baie Lazare, southwest coast)
credentials: Hilton's LXR Hotels & Resorts, the group's Seychelles property
MICHELIN Guide hotel selection (a hotel listing, not a dining star)
items.description: The former home of Italian photographer Gian Paolo Barbieri reborn as a design-led boutique retreat, the most stylish, character-rich address on Mahé.

items.name: Vallée de Mai, the primeval palm forest
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Vallée de Mai Nature Reserve (inscribed 1983)
items.description: A UNESCO-listed valley where you walk through a forest almost unchanged since prehistory, the world's last great stand of the coco de mer palm, whose 20kg double-lobed nut is the largest seed on Earth and whose suggestive shape once fed legends that this was the original Garden of Eden. Go early with a naturalist guide, listen for the rare Seychelles black parrot found nowhere else, and let the cathedral hush of the primeval forest do the rest.

items.name: Anse Source d'Argent, the granite-boulder beach
items.description: The most photographed beach in the world, a string of shallow, glass-clear coves screened by sculpted pink granite boulders 750 million years old, reached on foot through the L'Union Estate coconut plantation. Come at low tide in the soft late-afternoon light, ideally by bicycle from the jetty, for the barefoot, camera-in-hand honeymoon picture the Seychelles is famous for.

items.name: Anse Lazio, Praslin's crescent
credentials: Repeatedly ranked among the world's best beaches (TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice; CNN)
items.description: A wide arc of powder sand framed by takamaka trees and warm granite, repeatedly ranked among the best beaches on the planet by CNN and TripAdvisor and calm enough for a long swim off the rocks at either end. Arrive mid-morning before the day-trippers, take lunch at one of the two beach restaurants, and treat the whole afternoon as the definition of unhurried.

items.name: Anse Georgette, the hidden gem
credentials: Ranked among the world's 50 best beaches (World's 50 Beaches)
items.description: A perfect, near-empty white bay inside the grounds of Constance Lémuria, access is free but must be arranged in advance if you are not a resort guest, which keeps the crowds away and the sand pristine. For couples chasing the barefoot-billionaire seclusion the Seychelles promises, this is the quiet counterpoint to busier Anse Lazio.

items.name: Curieuse Island giant-tortoise day trip
items.description: A twenty-minute boat hop lands you on a russet-earthed island where some 300 free-roaming Aldabra giant tortoises graze among the mangroves and a boardwalk threads a rare coco-de-mer-and-mangrove landscape. Pair it with a Creole barbecue lunch on the sand and a snorkel stop; a private charter turns a good excursion into an unhurried, uncrowded one.

items.name: St Pierre islet snorkelling
items.description: A picture-book cluster of granite boulders crowned with palms, ringed by some of Praslin's clearest water and busiest reef fish, the classic snorkel stop on a Curieuse day trip. Charter a private boat to arrive before the group excursions and you may have the whole jewel-like islet to yourselves.

items.name: Cousin Island seabird sanctuary
items.description: A strictly protected conservation island reached only on a guided landing, where thousands of nesting seabirds, hawksbill turtles and the once-vanishing Seychelles magpie-robin have been brought back from the brink. Visitor numbers are capped and mornings only, a rare, deeply intimate wildlife encounter for travellers who value pristine nature over crowds.

items.name: Aride Island, the northernmost bird island
items.description: The Seychelles' most important seabird island, over a million birds and the largest colonies of some species on Earth, landing on a wild, roadless nature reserve open only a few days a week and closed in the roughest season. A private boat and a calm-sea day make it one of the archipelago's great, little-seen natural spectacles.

items.name: Beau Vallon beach
items.description: Mahé's long, easy, palm-backed north-coast bay, the most reliable place on the island for a proper year-round swim, with sunset paddleboarding, a Wednesday-evening bazaar and casual Creole grills a short stroll away. An unfussy home base for a family who want the sea on the doorstep rather than a trek to a wild cove.

items.name: Anse Intendance, the wild south beach
items.description: A broad, undeveloped stretch of white sand and rolling surf in Mahé's untamed south, framed by granite headlands and backed only by takamaka trees, the beach beside Banyan Tree and among the most dramatic on the island. Magnificent for a long walk and a photograph; the currents are strong when the trade winds blow, so it's for watching the ocean's power more than swimming.

items.name: Anse Takamaka
items.description: A gently curving south-coast bay of pale sand and clear water named for the shade trees that line it, famous for its sunsets and, on calm days, its snorkelling. Chez Batista on the sand serves grilled fish with your toes in the sand, the essence of a slow Mahé afternoon.

items.name: Petite Anse
items.description: A flawless, sheltered cove within the Four Seasons estate but open to the public, reached down a short forest path, with soft powdery sand and gentle water that make it one of the south coast's most swimmable beaches. A discreet, resort-tended stretch of sand for couples who want beauty without the trek.

items.name: Anse Soleil & Anse Soleil beach
items.description: A tiny, boulder-flanked south-western cove at the end of a steep road, with excellent snorkelling straight off the sand and a beloved barefoot Creole café above it. Small, sheltered and gloriously out of the way, the reward for a driver who knows the back lanes of Baie Lazare.

items.name: Sir Selwyn Selwyn-Clarke Market
items.description: The beating heart of the tiny capital since 1840, a covered market piled with tropical fruit, vanilla pods, cinnamon bark, chilli and the morning's reef catch, best at 8am when the fishmongers set out. A short, sensory, grounding stop between beaches, and the place to understand how Creole, African, Indian and French flavours met on these islands.

items.name: The Clock Tower (Little Big Ben)
items.description: The silver Victorian clock tower erected in 1903 at the crossroads of the capital, modelled on a London original and the postcard symbol of Victoria, one of the smallest capital cities in the world. A five-minute stroll takes in the tower, the market and the Hindu temple; a gentle way to feel the island's colonial layer.

items.name: Arul Mihu Navasakthi Vinayagar Temple
items.description: The only Hindu temple in the Seychelles, a vividly painted gopuram on Quincy Street, built in 1992 and dedicated to Lord Vinayagar (Ganesha), serving the island's small Tamil-descended community. A moment of the familiar for Indian travellers, and a reminder of how far the diaspora and its gods have travelled across the Indian Ocean.

items.name: Seychelles National Botanical Gardens
items.description: A century-old garden on the edge of the capital with 200-plus species, coco de mer palms, a spice grove, orchids, a colony of fruit bats and a paddock of feedable Aldabra giant tortoises. A cool, shaded, easy hour for grandparents and children alike, a short drive from the harbour.

items.name: The National Museum of History
items.description: The capital's museum of Seychelles history housed in a restored colonial building, the Stone of Possession that claimed the islands for France, pirate lore, and the Creole story of settlement, slavery and independence. A short, well-curated context stop for travellers who like to understand a place before they lie on its beaches.

items.name: Morne Seychellois National Park
items.description: The mist-forested spine of Mahé, a protected mountain wilderness of cloud forest, endemic pitcher plants and hidden trails climbing to the island's 905m high point. The wild green heart behind the beaches, best explored on foot with a guide who can read the endemic flora.

items.name: The Copolia Trail
items.description: The island's most rewarding short hike, an hour through shaded palm forest to a bald granite dome at nearly 500m, with an eagle's-eye sweep over Victoria, the Sainte Anne islands and, on a clear day, Praslin and La Digue. Manageable for most fitness levels and the single best view on Mahé for the effort.

items.name: Morne Blanc & the Tea Factory
items.description: A steep, short nature trail climbing to a sheer-drop lookout over Mahé's west coast, beginning near the little hillside tea plantation that has grown Seychelles tea since 1962. Combine the walk with a stop at the tea factory shop for vanilla and citronella teas, a fragrant, cool interlude high above the sea.

items.name: Sauzier Waterfall (Port Launay)
items.description: A ten-minute walk through a private garden brings you to a jungle waterfall tumbling into a cool freshwater pool you can swim in, a rare, refreshing counterpoint to the salt and the sun. Easy enough for children, quiet enough for couples, and a lovely hidden gem near the west-coast beaches.

items.name: Mission Lodge (Venn's Town) viewpoint
items.description: The ruins of a 19th-century school for the children of freed slaves, high on the Sans Souci road, with a hilltop gazebo built for Queen Elizabeth II's 1972 visit that frames a sweeping view of Mahé's forested west. A poignant piece of history and one of the island's most cinematic viewpoints in a single easy stop.

items.name: Takamaka Rum Distillery, La Plaine St André
items.description: The island's craft rum distillery set in a restored 1792 plantation house, with guided tours, tastings, resident giant tortoises named Taka and Maka, a garden restaurant and Friday-night cocktails and live music. A relaxed, characterful half-day and the obvious place to taste, and take home, the Seychelles' signature spirit.

items.name: Domaine de Val des Prés craft village
items.description: A cluster of traditional wooden Creole houses restored as artisan workshops, model boat-builders, jewellers, potters and a plantation-house restaurant serving classic island cooking. The most tangible taste of old Creole life and craft on Mahé, and a good place to buy something genuinely local.

items.name: Baie Lazare & the south-western coves
items.description: A sleepy fishing village that gives its name to the loveliest tangle of coves in Mahé's south-west, the gateway to Anse Soleil, Petite Anse and Anse Gaulette, with a hilltop church and Creole eateries. The area to base a day of unhurried cove-hopping with a private driver.

items.name: Anse Royale
items.description: A long, reef-protected east-coast beach with calm, shallow water ideal for family swimming and snorkelling at the little offshore island, backed by a friendly village and casual takeaways. An easygoing, local-feeling stretch that balances Mahé's wilder south beaches.

items.name: Eden Island
items.description: A modern marina-and-residence development off Victoria with waterfront restaurants, a small mall and the archipelago's main yacht berths, the practical launch point for many private charters and a pleasant evening stroll and dinner by the boats. Useful and comfortable rather than wild, and where a chartered yacht will likely meet you.

items.name: Grand Anse & Petite Anse, La Digue
items.description: La Digue's dramatic south-east coast, Grand Anse a wide, powerful surf beach and, over the headland on foot, the quieter, more sheltered Petite Anse and Anse Cocos. A beautiful, breezy bicycle-and-walking loop through the island's wild side, best when the sea is calm from October to April.

items.name: The ox-cart & bicycle island life of La Digue
items.description: An island with almost no cars, where the traditional way to travel is by bicycle or ox-cart along sandy lanes past pastel Creole houses and vanilla plantations. Renting a good bike for the day is the whole point of La Digue, the slowest, most charming pace in the Seychelles.

items.name: Nid d'Aigle viewpoint
items.description: The 'Eagle's Nest', La Digue's 333m high point, reached by a steep track (best by hired local transport for part of the way, then on foot) to a panorama over the island's granite peaks and the turquoise channel to Praslin. The reward for the effort is the finest view in the inner islands.

items.name: L'Union Estate, La Digue
items.description: The historic coconut-and-vanilla plantation you pass through to reach Anse Source d'Argent, an old copra mill turned by an ox, a colonial plantation house, a vanilla plot and a pen of giant tortoises. A living slice of 19th-century island life that adds depth to the world's most photographed beach.

items.name: Sainte Anne Marine National Park
items.description: The Indian Ocean's first marine park, six islands just off Victoria, with over 150 species in the clear channels, easy snorkelling among hawksbill turtles and reef fish, and glass-bottom-boat trips for those who prefer to stay dry. A gentle, family-friendly introduction to the underwater Seychelles, minutes from the capital.

items.name: Diving the inner islands
items.description: Warm, clear water over granite drop-offs, wrecks and reefs alive with turtles, rays, whale sharks in season and the occasional reef shark, with reputable dive centres on Mahé and Praslin catering to first dives and log-book veterans alike. The archipelago's granite topography makes for some of the Indian Ocean's most atmospheric diving.

items.name: Whale-shark encounters (seasonal)
items.description: Between roughly August and October the world's largest fish gathers off Mahé's coast, and licensed operators run respectful swim-alongside snorkel trips to meet these gentle giants. A once-in-a-lifetime, strictly seasonal experience, worth timing a trip around for wildlife-minded travellers.

items.name: Turtle nesting & hatching (seasonal)
items.description: Hawksbill turtles nest by day on Seychelles beaches from roughly October to February, and on conservation-minded islands and resorts guests can quietly watch a female lay or, weeks later, hatchlings scramble to the sea. A tender, protected wildlife moment that the best luxury islands build guided programmes around.

items.name: Deep-sea game fishing
items.description: The drop-offs and banks off the Seychelles hold sailfish, marlin, wahoo, dogtooth tuna and giant trevally, some of the Indian Ocean's finest big-game and fly-fishing, from half-day trolls to serious blue-water charters. A private boat with a seasoned skipper turns it into a bespoke day at sea.

items.name: Private yacht & catamaran charter
items.description: The most luxurious way to see the Seychelles is to sail it, a crewed catamaran or motor yacht out of Eden Island, anchoring off empty beaches, snorkelling deserted reefs and dining on deck as the sun goes down. Complete privacy, your own itinerary, and the barefoot seclusion the islands are made for.

items.name: Island-hopping by helicopter
items.description: Zil Air's air-conditioned helicopters connect Mahé, Praslin, La Digue and the private-island resorts in minutes, with scenic flights that reveal the archipelago's turquoise lagoons and granite peaks from above. The fastest, most spectacular way for time-short travellers to string the best of the islands together, or to arrive at a private island in style.

items.name: A day at a private-island resort
items.description: The Seychelles' defining ultra-luxury experience, a whole island to a handful of guests, whether North Island's barefoot villas, Six Senses Zil Pasyon on Félicité, Frégate with its wild tortoise colonies or Cousine's conservation reserve. The pinnacle of the private-island escape, reached by boat or helicopter, where the beach outside your villa may be entirely your own.

items.name: Fond Ferdinand Nature Reserve
items.description: A less-visited, guided alternative to the Vallée de Mai, a steep-sided reserve with an even larger stand of coco de mer palms and, from its ridge, a rare panoramic view over Praslin and out to the neighbouring islands. Quieter and more strenuous, it rewards travellers who want the coco de mer forest with fewer people.

items.name: Côte d'Or (Anse Volbert)
items.description: Praslin's long, calm, palm-lined main beach, safe for swimming, dotted with beach restaurants and dive shops, and the departure point for boats to Curieuse, St Pierre and the bird islands. The convenient, easygoing base for a Praslin stay, with plenty for families.

items.name: Creole cuisine & a spice-trail lunch
items.description: Seychellois cooking is a fragrant crossroads, grilled bourgeois and job-fish, octopus curry, coconut and breadfruit, tamarind and chilli, and Indian palates find the spicing gloriously familiar, with good vegetarian and Indian options at the larger resorts. A long lunch at a beachside Creole table is as much a highlight here as any view.

items.name: A signature island spa ritual
items.description: The luxury resorts, Four Seasons, Constance, Six Senses, Raffles, North Island, build spas around treetop pavilions and clifftop decks, using local coconut, vanilla and frangipani in barefoot rituals to the sound of the sea. The unhurried, restorative core of a Seychelles honeymoon or escape.

items.name: '20 Degrees Sud'
credentials: Anantara Maia's award-winning signature restaurant
items.description: Anantara Maia's signature table, a hilltop or intimate wine-cellar setting for Creole-Mediterranean cooking and hard-to-find wines, the most refined dining experience on the main island.

items.name: ZEZ
items.area: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles, Mahé (Petite Anse)
credentials: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles' signature dinner venue (Forbes Four-Star resort)
items.description: Four Seasons' hilltop restaurant, high above the bay, an inventive sharing menu at night with one of the best ocean views on the island.

items.name: Kannel
items.area: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles, Mahé (Petite Anse)
credentials: Four Seasons Resort Seychelles restaurant (Forbes Four-Star resort)
items.description: Beachside all-day dining at the Four Seasons, marrying Mediterranean flavours with Creole tradition, ceviches and salads by day, seafood and pasta by night.

items.name: Marie Antoinette
items.area: Mahé (Serret Road, St Louis, above Victoria)
credentials: One of the oldest and most celebrated Creole restaurants in the Seychelles (est. 1972); a long-standing press and guidebook fixture
items.description: The islands' most storied Creole table, a set feast of parrotfish, tuna, aubergine fritters and chicken curry served in a colonial planter's house since 1972.

items.name: Del Place
credentials: A long-running west-coast Creole seafood institution, widely recommended in Seychelles dining guides
items.description: A seafront Creole seafood house on the quiet west coast, tables almost in the water, with sunsets over the neighbouring islands.

items.name: La Plage
credentials: A landmark restaurant on Beau Vallon, the Seychelles' best-known beach, and a fixture of local dining guides
items.description: Feet-in-the-sand Italian-Creole cooking on the island's most famous beach, the archetypal Beau Vallon sundowner-and-dinner.

items.name: Boardwalk Bar & Grill
credentials: The marquee bar-and-grill on Eden Island, the Seychelles' upmarket marina development
items.description: The marina-side gathering point on Eden Island, waterfront tables, live music and a late bar, the most reliable evening scene outside the resorts.

items.name: Boat House
credentials: A long-established Beau Vallon dining-and-bar landmark
items.description: A Beau Vallon institution pairing a Creole buffet with a lively bar and live music, the beach's social anchor after dark.

items.name: The resort bars
credentials: Credentialed by the resorts themselves, see the Forbes, Condé Nast and maison hotels listed above
items.description: The honest truth of Seychelles nights: the best-made drink you'll have is almost always at your own resort, a sunset villa deck, a spa-hotel bar or an island long bar.

items.name: Katiolo
items.area: Mahé (Anse Faure, east coast, near the airport)
credentials: The Seychelles' longest-running and best-known nightclub, the only beachside disco in the country
items.description: The Seychelles' oldest and most iconic nightclub, an open-air dancefloor by the sea, and about as close as the islands get to a genuine late night out.

plan.heading: 4 days in Mahé, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at Mahé and settle at Four Seasons at Petite Anse or the North Island's sister on the coast.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The long granite-boulder curve of Beau Vallon or Anse Soleil, an easy first swim.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at the resort, creole-inflected seafood and a Takamaka rum after.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The small capital, the clock tower, the Sir Selwyn Selwyn-Clarke market, and the Hindu temple.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Up to the Morne Seychellois trails or the tea plantation on the hill road, then back to the coast.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet table at Marie Antoinette, the old creole house restaurant in Victoria.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private boat to Sainte Anne Marine Park or across to Praslin's Anse Lazio, snorkelling the reef.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Vallée de Mai on Praslin, the primeval palm forest of the coco de mer, walked with a guide.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Return to Mahé for a beachfront dinner as the light goes.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A slow morning at Anse Intendance or Petite Anse, the surf and the boulders, with a long swim.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A spa treatment and an unhurried lunch before packing.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at the resort, the Indian Ocean dark beyond the terrace, before the morning flight.

items.name: Beau Vallon
items.description: The main north beach, with the most restaurants and dive shops; convenient but busiest.

items.name: The south coast (Takamaka/Intendance)
items.description: Quiet, dramatic beaches and a few discreet lodges; for seclusion over amenities.

items.name: Victoria & Eden Island
items.description: The tiny capital and its marina; a practical base near the airport and ferries, not the beaches.

events.name: Festival Kreol
events.note: The country's biggest cultural festival, Creole music, food and dance across a week.

events.name: Carnaval International de Victoria
events.note: A colourful international parade through the capital celebrating the islands' mixed heritage.

events.name: SUBIOS Underwater Festival
events.note: A celebration of Seychelles' marine heritage with film, exhibitions and dive events.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in the northwest around Beau Vallon for beaches and dining or a private-island resort for total seclusion; it's low-key and barefoot-luxury in tone, the sun is fierce so plan water and shade, and the granite beaches (Anse Source d'Argent, Anse Intendance) are the ones worth the effort.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Seychelles International (SEZ) on Mahé; a private car transfer reaches most of the island within 30–45 minutes, while a helicopter or short Air Seychelles hop connects you to Praslin, La Digue or a private-island resort.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver suits Mahé's winding coast roads; for island-hopping use scheduled helicopters, the Cat Cocos fast ferry, or your resort's boat.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An Airtel or Cable & Wireless eSIM gives good 4G on the main islands; resort wifi is reliable, coverage thins on remote islets.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Seychellois rupee (SCR); cards are widely accepted and euros often quoted at resorts, with a 5–10 percent tip appreciated where service isn't added.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: April-May and October-November are the calm, in-between sweet spots with light winds and clear water. The May to September southeast trade winds bring breezier seas and seaweed on some beaches, while December to March is hotter, wetter and humid.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Mumbai (~4h30m) on Air India a few times weekly; otherwise connect via Colombo on SriLankan/Air Seychelles (~4h Colombo-Mahé) or via the Gulf on Emirates/Etihad/Qatar in first or business. The Gulf carriers offer the finest premium cabins, and a Colombo routing pairs naturally with a Sri Lanka stopover.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations from India (yellow-fever certificate only if transiting an endemic country); routine jabs sufficient. Tap water on Mahé is generally safe, bottled is easy to find. Very safe and private, a favoured discreet escape; no altitude concerns.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Manageable but less abundant than Mauritius; Creole cuisine is fish-forward, so vegetarians should lean on hotels, which cater well. Strict Jain travellers should arrange menus in advance with the resort (North Island, Four Seasons, Six Senses Zil Pasyon all accommodate), and Indian options exist but are limited off-property.
